question: A retailer needs to predict next week’s revenue in rand for each store using historical sales and promotions. Managers will later label each prediction as above or below target. Which technique should produce the revenue estimate?
options: A. Classification into revenue bands | B. Regression on historical sales and promotions | C. Clustering stores by sales patterns | D. Anomaly detection on weekly revenue
why: Regression predicts the numeric revenue amount. The later above/below-target label is a separate calculation using that prediction.
all_option_reasons: A. Classification predicts a category or band, rather than the requested revenue amount. | B. Regression learns a relationship between input features and a numeric target such as revenue. | C. Clustering groups similar stores without directly learning the requested revenue target. | D. Anomaly detection identifies unusual observations rather than predicting the expected revenue amount.
clues: revenue in rand: The model must estimate an amount, not a group or label.
hint: Identify the output required before the manager applies the target rule.
trap: Choosing a technique for the downstream label instead of the requested prediction.
transfer: Predicting a lease payment amount is regression; predicting whether a lease will default is classification.

question: A model learns from emails already marked spam or safe. What is this?
options: A. Unsupervised learning | B. Reinforcement learning | C. Supervised learning | D. Pre-training only
why: Supervised learning uses labeled examples. The spam labels supply the target answers.
all_option_reasons: A. Unsupervised learning discovers structure without target labels. | B. Reinforcement learning uses feedback about actions and rewards, not just labeled email examples. | C. Supervised learning maps examples to known target labels. | D. Pre-training describes a training stage, not the best description of these labeled examples.
clues: already marked: Known target labels are available during training.
hint: Ask whether the desired answers are supplied with the examples.
trap: Spam is the application; labeled examples determine the learning type.
transfer: A labeled support-ticket set can train a model to predict the ticket category.

question: Which metric matters most when missing actual fraud is especially costly?
options: A. Recall | B. Precision | C. Accuracy | D. F1 score
why: Recall measures the proportion of actual fraud cases detected, directly addressing missed positives.
all_option_reasons: A. Recall measures the proportion of actual fraud cases detected, directly addressing missed positives. | B. Precision measures how trustworthy positive fraud alerts are, rather than how many actual fraud cases were missed. | C. Accuracy can be dominated by legitimate transactions when fraud is rare. | D. F1 balances precision and recall; the stated priority specifically emphasizes missed fraud and therefore recall.
clues: missing actual fraud: False negatives are the error the business most wants to reduce.
hint: Focus on the costliest error, not a generic overall score.
trap: High accuracy can hide missed fraud when most transactions are legitimate.
transfer: A cancer-screening model should be checked for the share of actual cases it detects.

question: Which AWS service converts recorded speech into text?
options: A. Amazon Polly | B. Amazon Translate | C. Amazon Comprehend | D. Amazon Transcribe
why: Transcribe recognizes speech. Polly does the reverse: text to speech.
all_option_reasons: A. Polly generates speech from text, the reverse direction. | B. Translate converts text between languages. | C. Comprehend analyzes text; it does not transcribe audio. | D. Transcribe converts speech recordings into text.
clues: speech into text: Check the direction of conversion.
hint: Identify what goes in and what must come out.
trap: Polly and Transcribe are easy to reverse: read the input/output direction.
transfer: Recorded meeting audio needs transcription before it can be searched as text.

question: Which TWO tasks should primarily use deterministic rules rather than a probabilistic model?
options: A. Group customers by similar purchasing behavior | B. Calculate a tax amount using an exact published formula | C. Recognize objects in product photographs | D. Enforce whether an identity has permission to read a restricted object | E. Forecast next month’s sales
why: Exact formulas and permission enforcement require rule-based outcomes, while clustering, vision and forecasting can benefit from learned predictions.
all_option_reasons: A. Grouping by similarity can use ML clustering. | B. An exact formula should be computed directly rather than estimated. | C. Object recognition is a common computer-vision task. | D. Authorization must be enforced by a policy decision, not guessed by a model. | E. Forecasting unknown future values is a common prediction task.
clues: deterministic rules: Choose tasks requiring exact calculation or an enforced access decision.
hint: Look for exact outcomes, and select exactly two tasks.
trap: A model may help describe a rule, but it should not replace the calculation or authorization control.
transfer: A precise payroll formula and an access rule should be enforced rather than estimated.

question: A team uses a model priced per input token. Two prompts ask the same question with different wording. Their word counts are equal, but their quoted input costs differ. Which measurement best explains the difference?
options: A. The number of user requests submitted | B. The number of complete words supplied | C. The number of tokens produced by the model’s tokenizer | D. The number of characters displayed to the user
why: Token-based input pricing uses the token count for the selected model. Equal word counts do not guarantee equal token counts.
all_option_reasons: A. Both prompts are single requests; request count does not explain different input-token charges. | B. A word may be represented by one or several tokens, so equal word counts can have different costs. | C. The tokenizer determines the model’s input units, which are used for the stated pricing model. | D. Character counts can be a rough proxy but are not the billing unit in this scenario.
clues: priced per input token: The measurement must match the stated pricing unit.
hint: Use the provider’s stated billing unit rather than a convenient text-length estimate.
trap: Treating one word as exactly one token, or confusing input cost with the total bill.
transfer: Changing languages or including code can change token counts even when the request means the same thing.

question: A search app needs to find passages that mean something similar to a user’s query even when they use different words. What representation should it compare?
options: A. Encrypted copies of the query and passages | B. Numeric embedding vectors of the query and passages | C. The number of tokens billed for each passage | D. The model’s claimed confidence in its generated answer
why: Embedding vectors can be compared to retrieve semantically related content.
all_option_reasons: A. Encryption protects data but does not provide semantic similarity values. | B. Embeddings represent features numerically for vector similarity search. | C. Token counts measure input length, not meaning. | D. A generated confidence claim is not a passage representation.
clues: different words: Exact word matching can miss related meaning.
hint: Look for a representation designed for semantic similarity rather than storage or billing.
trap: Treating a vector as encryption or a guarantee that a retrieved passage is correct.
transfer: “How do I cancel?” may retrieve a passage headed “termination procedure” through semantic vector similarity.

question: A chatbot invents a believable citation. What is this called?
options: A. Data poisoning | B. Prompt injection | C. Hallucination | D. Model distillation
why: Fabricating a plausible citation is an example of hallucination: generated content without factual support.
all_option_reasons: A. Data poisoning corrupts training or source data; the scenario describes an unsupported generated assertion. | B. Prompt injection involves instructions trying to redirect the system; no such attack is described. | C. Fabricating a plausible citation is an example of hallucination: generated content without factual support. | D. Distillation trains a smaller model from a teacher and is not the name for fabricated content.
clues: invents a believable citation: The output sounds credible but lacks factual support.
hint: Distinguish fluent wording from verified evidence.
trap: Do not treat a plausible citation as a checked source.
transfer: A generated legal reference should be verified against the actual source before use.

question: A product team wants managed API access to foundation models from several providers and will select a model at request time. Which AWS service is the primary model-access layer?
options: A. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases | B. Amazon SageMaker JumpStart | C. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime | D. Amazon Bedrock
why: Amazon Bedrock supplies the managed foundation-model access requested.
all_option_reasons: A. Knowledge Bases adds retrieval for applications; it is not the general multi-provider model API. | B. JumpStart helps discover and deploy pretrained models, but the scenario asks for the managed model API layer. | C. AgentCore Runtime runs agents and tools, not the primary model catalogue/inference service. | D. Bedrock provides managed access to foundation models from multiple providers.
clues: managed API access to foundation models from several providers: The requirement is model invocation, not retrieval or agent hosting.
hint: Distinguish the model access layer from tools that can surround it.
trap: Choosing a related Bedrock capability simply because it also appears in an AI application.
transfer: A team may compare provider models through Bedrock before adding a document knowledge base.

question: An internal assistant must connect to tools, respect access limits, use changing policies and adopt a response style. Match each requirement to the most direct concept. Use each option once.
options: A. IAM authorization | B. Fine-tuning | C. Model Context Protocol (MCP) | D. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
why: MCP connects tools, IAM authorizes access, RAG supplies retrieved context and fine-tuning adapts model weights. These capabilities can complement one another.
all_option_reasons: A. IAM policies control permitted actions on AWS resources; a tool connection does not grant those permissions. | B. Fine-tuning adapts weights using training examples; it is different from inserting documents into a prompt. | C. MCP standardizes connections to external tools and context; authorization is still needed. | D. RAG retrieves relevant source material for the current request without retraining the foundation model.
clues: most direct concept: Match each responsibility rather than choosing an entire architecture.
hint: Distinguish connection, permission, runtime information and training.
trap: Assuming that connecting a tool authorizes it, or that retrieving a document trains the model.
transfer: A connected expense tool still needs access checks; retrieving its latest policy does not change the model’s weights.

question: An employee assistant must answer from a large policy library that changes daily and show supporting passages. The team will keep its existing foundation model. Which design best meets both requirements?
options: A. Retrieve relevant passages from a synchronized policy index and attach source references | B. Fine-tune weekly on the policies and ask the model to name its sources | C. Cache generated policy answers and refresh them after users report changes | D. Add a link to the policy website in the system prompt without retrieving its content
why: RAG can supply current, relevant policy passages and their source references at answer time. The source-to-index synchronization must also stay current.
all_option_reasons: A. Retrieval from an updated index supplies both current evidence and traceable passages. | B. Weekly training can lag daily changes, and naming a source is not evidence that its passage was retrieved. | C. Cached answers can remain stale until a user notices; they do not meet the requirement for current supporting passages. | D. A URL alone does not give the model access to the page or retrieve supporting text.
clues: changes daily: The information pipeline must reflect updates. | supporting passages: The answer needs retrieved evidence, not just a source name.
hint: Check how each approach obtains updated evidence and makes it traceable.
trap: Assuming that a generated citation or a current-looking URL proves the answer is grounded.
transfer: For a changing product catalogue, refresh retrieval data and check grounding; retraining alone does not supply current source passages.

question: A prompt includes three examples of the desired response. Which technique is used?
options: A. Zero-shot | B. Distillation | C. Few-shot | D. Pre-training
why: Few-shot prompting supplies examples in context. It does not update model weights.
all_option_reasons: A. Zero-shot prompting does not supply task demonstrations. | B. Distillation trains a student to learn from a teacher model. | C. Few-shot prompting uses a small number of examples in context. | D. Pre-training learns model parameters from a broad training corpus.
clues: three examples: The prompt demonstrates the desired behavior.
hint: Count examples in the prompt, not model parameters.
trap: Examples in a prompt are not automatically fine-tuning.
transfer: Two example replies in a request can demonstrate the desired style without training.

question: Repeated runs of the same summarization prompt produce too much variation. The model exposes temperature and a maximum-output-token setting. The team wants less sampling randomness while retaining room for a complete summary. Which change best fits?
options: A. Lower temperature while keeping the output-token budget unchanged | B. Lower the output-token budget while keeping temperature unchanged | C. Add stop sequences while keeping temperature unchanged | D. Cache the first summary and reuse it for every later document
why: Lower temperature generally favors higher-probability next tokens, reducing sampling variation without directly shortening the output allowance.
all_option_reasons: A. This adjusts sampling randomness while preserving room for the summary; it does not guarantee identical or factual responses. | B. The token budget limits length and may truncate a summary, rather than directly controlling sampling randomness. | C. Stop sequences terminate generation at specified text; they do not directly adjust the sampling distribution. | D. Reusing one answer for different documents can return the wrong summary and does not tune generation.
clues: less sampling randomness: The requested behavior is controlled by a sampling parameter.
hint: Distinguish a sampling control from a length control or response reuse.
trap: Assuming less randomness guarantees truth, or reducing length when the problem is variability.
transfer: For repeated extraction tasks, lower temperature may improve consistency, but schema validation and factual checks remain necessary.

question: A team wants a smaller model to learn from a larger model’s outputs. What is this?
options: A. Few-shot prompting | B. Retrieval-augmented generation | C. Prompt caching | D. Model distillation
why: Distillation trains a smaller student to learn from a larger teacher model.
all_option_reasons: A. Few-shot prompting supplies examples at inference time without training a student model. | B. RAG retrieves source material for context and does not itself train a student. | C. Prompt caching reuses supported processing of repeated context rather than transferring model capabilities. | D. Distillation trains a smaller student to learn from a larger teacher model.
clues: smaller model: A smaller student is learning from a larger teacher.
hint: Distinguish training a student from retrieving documents.
trap: Do not confuse distillation with compressing a prompt.
transfer: A smaller student model can be trained using responses from a larger teacher.

question: A support agent answers questions fluently but customers still abandon cases when the agent cannot complete a required handoff. Which evaluation best measures whether the application meets the business goal?
options: A. Measure completed cases, successful handoffs, user satisfaction and cost on representative cases | B. Measure response helpfulness alone on a generic benchmark | C. Measure the agent’s retrieval accuracy without checking the handoff | D. Measure the foundation model’s raw token speed without task outcomes
why: Evaluate the full workflow against business outcomes and cost, not only a component’s output quality.
all_option_reasons: A. End-to-end cases and handoffs, with quality and cost, reflect the actual objective. | B. Helpfulness on unrelated prompts can miss failure in the business workflow. | C. Retrieval quality matters, but a correct document does not prove the handoff completes. | D. Tokens per second can affect latency but cannot establish task completion.
clues: cannot complete a required handoff: The failure occurs after a plausible answer, at the workflow boundary.
hint: Identify what a successful case requires beyond a good response.
trap: Treating a fluent response or good retrieval result as completed customer work.
transfer: A travel agent is useful when the booking completes correctly, not merely when its itinerary sounds helpful.

question: A hiring model has high overall accuracy. One demographic group reports more mistaken rejections, but few members of that group appear in the evaluation data. What is the best first investigation?
options: A. Compare average model confidence across all applicants | B. Compare subgroup false-rejection rates and whether each sample supports a reliable conclusion | C. Remove demographic labels from the evaluation data and repeat the aggregate score | D. Apply the same decision threshold to every group and report the original accuracy
why: Subgroup error rates investigate the reported harm, while sample adequacy determines how confidently those rates can be compared.
all_option_reasons: A. Overall confidence can conceal subgroup errors and is not a measure of the reported false rejections. | B. This directly investigates the reported error and the strength of the supporting evidence. | C. Removing labels prevents the proposed subgroup comparison; it does not establish fairness. | D. A common threshold alone does not establish comparable error rates or fix an inadequate evaluation sample.
clues: mistaken rejections: Investigate the relevant error, not confidence alone. | few members: A small sample can make comparisons unreliable.
hint: Measure the reported harm for the affected group, then check the strength of the evidence.
trap: Treating equal thresholds, confidence or aggregate accuracy as proof of fairness.
transfer: A service can score well overall while working poorly for a language or region with little evaluation data.

question: A loan model declines an application. A reviewer needs to explain which factors influenced this specific result without promising that the model is always right. Which capability helps most?
options: A. A model card describing intended use for the model as a whole | B. A case-level explanation of influential inputs, checked for its limits | C. A CloudTrail record of who invoked an API | D. A precision score aggregated across all applicants
why: Case-level explainability helps interpret influential factors in an individual prediction; it does not prove the decision is correct or fair.
all_option_reasons: A. A model card helps document overall use and limitations, but not necessarily this case’s factors. | B. A case-level explanation can help interpret this outcome while still requiring validation. | C. An API event log shows activity, not why the prediction was made. | D. An aggregate metric does not explain the individual result.
clues: this specific result: The reviewer needs reasons relevant to one outcome.
hint: Distinguish a local explanation from a model-wide record or performance metric.
trap: Treating aggregate performance or general model documentation as an explanation for a specific decision.
transfer: A denied claim can show which submitted facts influenced the recommendation while preserving a human appeal.

question: Which feature helps filter harmful content in a Bedrock application?
options: A. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails | B. AWS Identity and Access Management | C. AWS CloudTrail | D. Amazon Macie
why: Bedrock Guardrails provides configurable content safeguards, which should be evaluated alongside other controls.
all_option_reasons: A. Bedrock Guardrails provides configurable content safeguards, which should be evaluated alongside other controls. | B. IAM controls authorization; it does not itself classify and filter generated harmful text. | C. CloudTrail supports auditing account activity rather than directly filtering a response. | D. Macie discovers sensitive data in S3; it is not the Bedrock response content-filter feature.
clues: filter harmful content: The required capability is a generation safeguard.
hint: Choose a control that acts on model input or output.
trap: Guardrails reduce risk; they are not an absolute safety guarantee.
transfer: A Bedrock application can evaluate both a user prompt and model response with Guardrails.

question: A marketing team plans to sell posters made with a generative image service. The source images and model terms have not been checked. What should the team do before commercial use?
options: A. Check whether the output looks original to a colleague | B. Assume generated images have no third-party rights because a model created them | C. Use the output if a content filter did not block it | D. Review input rights, service terms and intellectual-property risks for the intended use
why: Commercial use calls for a rights and risk review of the inputs, service terms and output before publication.
all_option_reasons: A. Appearance alone does not establish legal permission or ownership. | B. Generated content can still raise rights and contractual questions. | C. A safety filter is not an intellectual-property clearance process. | D. Input provenance, applicable terms and intended commercial use determine what needs review.
clues: source images and model terms have not been checked: The unresolved issue concerns permission and terms for the intended use.
hint: Find the action that addresses rights rather than visual quality or safety filtering.
trap: Treating a content filter or originality impression as proof of commercial rights.
transfer: A team using generated product packaging should review the rights to uploaded reference art and the service terms.

question: An AI system recommends whether to deny a high-impact benefit claim. Staff often accept its recommendation without checking source evidence. What design most directly improves responsible oversight?
options: A. Show a confidence number and automatically finalize high-confidence denials | B. Log recommendations for later audit but give staff no way to override them | C. Give reviewers the relevant evidence, authority to correct errors and a recorded review route | D. Use a larger model and remove staff review to reduce delays
why: Human oversight needs useful evidence and a real path to intervene, not a nominal reviewer.
all_option_reasons: A. Confidence is not a substitute for evidence or a meaningful human decision. | B. After-the-fact logs do not let reviewers prevent or correct a current error. | C. Usable evidence and correction authority make oversight operational. | D. A larger model can still make consequential mistakes.
clues: without checking source evidence: The human role currently lacks meaningful scrutiny.
hint: Find the control that lets a person detect and change a wrong decision before harm.
trap: Calling a process “human in the loop” when the person cannot evaluate or override it.
transfer: A claims reviewer should see the cited policy and disputed facts before finalizing a denial.

question: An AI application should access only its required S3 objects. Apply which principle?
options: A. Make the bucket publicly readable for easier access | B. Use least-privilege IAM permissions | C. Encrypt the bucket but grant broad read permissions | D. Give the application a shared administrator credential
why: Least privilege restricts permitted actions and resources to those required for the application.
all_option_reasons: A. Public access exceeds the application’s need and may expose objects to others. | B. Least privilege restricts permitted actions and resources to those required for the application. | C. Encryption protects data but does not justify giving an application excess authorization. | D. Administrator credentials exceed the required scope and weaken accountability when shared.
clues: only its required S3 objects: Scope access to the actual task.
hint: Look for the smallest sufficient permission boundary.
trap: An application needing access does not justify broad account permissions.
transfer: A document assistant should have read access only to the necessary S3 prefix.

question: Which AWS service records account API activity for auditing?
options: A. Amazon CloudWatch metrics only | B. AWS Config configuration history | C. AWS CloudTrail | D. AWS Artifact compliance reports
why: CloudTrail records supported account API events and related activity for audit and investigation.
all_option_reasons: A. Operational metrics are not a substitute for an account API activity audit trail. | B. Config tracks resource configuration; it does not replace the requested API event history. | C. CloudTrail records supported account API events and related activity for audit and investigation. | D. Artifact provides compliance documents rather than recording your account’s API calls.
clues: API activity: The requirement is an audit trail of account actions.
hint: Distinguish API auditing from model inference and text services.
trap: Logs serve different purposes; account activity is distinct from text generation.
transfer: A team can inspect CloudTrail events when investigating a changed AWS resource.

question: Which service helps discover sensitive data in Amazon S3?
options: A. Amazon Macie | B. AWS Key Management Service | C. AWS CloudTrail | D. AWS Identity and Access Management
why: Macie helps discover sensitive data in S3 objects.
all_option_reasons: A. Macie helps discover sensitive data in S3 objects. | B. KMS manages cryptographic keys; it does not perform the requested sensitive-content discovery. | C. CloudTrail records account activity, not a content classification scan of S3 objects. | D. IAM controls access permissions rather than discovering sensitive content.
clues: sensitive data in Amazon S3: The goal is identifying sensitive content in stored objects.
hint: Separate discovery of sensitive data from encryption of that data.
trap: Finding sensitive data is different from controlling who may read it.
transfer: Macie can help find sensitive records in S3 objects before they feed a model.

question: A retrieved document tells an agent to reveal secrets. What is the main threat?
options: A. An ordinary factual hallucination | B. A training underfitting problem | C. An output-length limit | D. Prompt injection
why: Prompt injection attempts to redirect an AI system through untrusted instructions, such as retrieved text.
all_option_reasons: A. The document is issuing hostile instructions rather than merely causing an unsupported factual statement. | B. Underfitting concerns inadequate learning and does not describe this instruction attack. | C. An output-length cap concerns generation size, not a request to reveal secrets. | D. Prompt injection attempts to redirect an AI system through untrusted instructions, such as retrieved text.
clues: retrieved document: The instructions are arriving through untrusted source content.
hint: Ask whether source data is being promoted into authority.
trap: RAG grounding does not make retrieved instructions trustworthy.
transfer: Instructions embedded in a retrieved web page should not be treated as authorized tool requests.

question: A team trains a model on a dataset assembled from three systems with filtering and corrections. Months later, it must explain why a specific source record was included. What should it maintain?
options: A. Only the final model accuracy report | B. Data lineage linking source records to transformation steps and dataset versions | C. Only the S3 object filename of the final dataset | D. Only the application’s inference latency logs
why: Data lineage records where information came from and how it changed.
all_option_reasons: A. Accuracy does not describe the data’s origins or changes. | B. Lineage links origin and transformations to the final dataset for traceability. | C. A filename lacks the upstream sources and processing history. | D. Inference latency is operational evidence, not training-data provenance.
clues: three systems with filtering and corrections: Several transformation steps need traceability.
hint: Choose a record that can trace the final training row back through its source and processing steps.
trap: Mistaking a final file name or performance score for data provenance.
transfer: A merged sales dataset should retain the source system and normalization history of each field.

question: A retailer groups customers by similar purchasing behavior without predefined segment labels. Which technique fits?
options: A. Regression | B. Clustering | C. Binary classification | D. Speech recognition
why: Clustering discovers groups based on similarity without predefined target labels.
all_option_reasons: A. Regression predicts a numeric target, not unlabeled groups. | B. Clustering discovers groups based on similarity without predefined target labels. | C. Binary classification needs a defined two-class target rather than unknown segments. | D. Speech recognition transcribes audio and is unrelated to this grouping task.
clues: without predefined segment labels: The groups are not known targets.
hint: Decide whether labels are given or groups must be discovered.
trap: Unlabeled does not automatically mean clustering; the grouping objective is also essential.
transfer: Group stores with similar sales patterns without supplying target group labels.

question: A spam filter raises false alarms on legitimate emails. Which metric directly asks how many predicted spam emails really are spam?
options: A. Recall | B. Accuracy | C. Precision | D. Mean absolute error
why: Precision measures actual positives among predicted positives, matching alert reliability.
all_option_reasons: A. Recall asks how many actual spam messages were found, not whether spam alerts are trustworthy. | B. Accuracy mixes correct spam and safe predictions and may hide the relevant error. | C. Precision measures actual positives among predicted positives, matching alert reliability. | D. Mean absolute error measures numeric prediction error, not class-alert reliability.
clues: predicted spam: The denominator is the set of positive predictions.
hint: Write out which group appears after the phrase out of.
trap: Precision and recall differ in their denominator, even when both discuss correct positives.
transfer: Review how many flagged messages are actually spam when false alerts are costly.

question: A classifier achieves excellent training results but performs poorly on unseen examples. What is the most likely issue?
options: A. Underfitting | B. Overfitting | C. Expected generalization | D. High inference latency
why: Strong training results with poor unseen performance suggest fitting training-specific patterns that do not generalize.
all_option_reasons: A. Underfitting generally produces inadequate performance even on the training data. | B. Strong training results with poor unseen performance suggest fitting training-specific patterns that do not generalize. | C. Expected generalization would produce adequate results on unseen examples too. | D. Latency is response time and does not explain the described training-versus-test quality gap.
clues: unseen examples: Generalization, not training memorization, is the concern.
hint: Compare training performance with performance on new data.
trap: More training accuracy alone can worsen the actual problem.
transfer: A model that memorizes training examples can falter on suitable new cases.

question: A team has defined a churn-prediction goal and collected historical records. Order the remaining stages so the final test data does not influence model selection. Use each stage once.
options: A. Train candidates and select settings using the training and validation sets | B. Deploy the accepted model and monitor real-world outcomes | C. Prepare suitable training, validation and untouched test sets | D. Evaluate the selected model on the untouched test set against acceptance criteria
why: Separate the data first, train and select using development data, evaluate on the untouched test set, then deploy only if acceptance criteria are met.
all_option_reasons: A. Training fits candidates; validation supports model selection without using final test results. | B. Deployment follows an acceptable evaluation, and monitoring checks real-world behavior. | C. Establish the splits before fitting; learn preprocessing parameters from training data and apply them to held-out data. | D. Use the untouched test set for final assessment after model selection, rather than repeatedly tuning to its results.
clues: final test data does not influence model selection: Keep the test set separate from training and validation.
hint: Identify when data must be reserved and which evidence should support the release decision.
trap: Selecting settings using the final test set, which makes the reported final assessment overly optimistic.
transfer: If you repeatedly change a prompt after reading its test results, reserve a fresh assessment set before claiming general performance.

question: A website needs a prediction while a customer is waiting at checkout. Which inference pattern fits best?
options: A. Nightly batch inference | B. Real-time inference | C. Offline model training | D. Historical data labeling
why: Real-time inference serves low-latency predictions for interactive requests.
all_option_reasons: A. Nightly batch processing does not return a result during the current checkout. | B. Real-time inference serves low-latency predictions for interactive requests. | C. Training creates or updates the model; it is not the live prediction step. | D. Labeling prepares examples rather than responding to the customer.
clues: while a customer is waiting: The result is needed during an interactive transaction.
hint: Identify the required response time before selecting a processing pattern.
trap: A prediction workload is not necessarily a training workload.
transfer: A checkout fraud decision needs a prediction during the transaction.

question: A company must score millions of stored records each night and deliver one output file before morning. No user waits for individual predictions. Which inference pattern is the most direct fit?
options: A. A synchronous endpoint invoked separately by a waiting user | B. An interactive streaming inference response | C. Batch inference over the stored dataset | D. Retrain the model for every record before predicting
why: Batch inference processes many stored inputs without a real-time response requirement.
all_option_reasons: A. A synchronous user path adds an immediate-response pattern the task does not need. | B. Streaming serves ongoing interactive output, not the requested overnight file job. | C. Batch processing fits a large dataset and deferred output. | D. Retraining per record is not an inference pattern for this requirement.
clues: millions of stored records each night: The workload is large and scheduled rather than interactive.
hint: Match the delivery time and input volume to the inference pattern.
trap: Assuming every prediction needs a live endpoint because the model is deployed.
transfer: A retailer can generate next-day demand scores for all stores overnight.

question: A mobile app must read a prepared text message aloud. Which AWS service fits?
options: A. Amazon Transcribe | B. Amazon Comprehend | C. Amazon Translate | D. Amazon Polly
why: Polly generates speech from text.
all_option_reasons: A. Transcribe turns speech into text, the reverse direction. | B. Comprehend analyzes text, such as sentiment or entities. | C. Translate converts languages but does not supply the requested speech output. | D. Polly generates speech from text.
clues: text message aloud: Text is the input; audio is the output.
hint: State the input and output formats before looking at the service names.
trap: Do not choose a speech-related service without checking the conversion direction.
transfer: An accessibility feature can speak a prepared article using Polly.

question: A game-playing model learns by taking actions and receiving rewards. Which learning approach fits?
options: A. Supervised learning from fixed class labels | B. Reinforcement learning | C. Unsupervised clustering | D. Numeric regression only
why: Reinforcement learning optimizes behavior based on interaction and rewards.
all_option_reasons: A. Fixed labeled examples differ from learning through actions and reward signals. | B. Reinforcement learning optimizes behavior based on interaction and rewards. | C. Clustering discovers groups rather than a rewarded action policy. | D. Regression predicts numbers; it does not describe the action-and-reward learning setup.
clues: actions and receiving rewards: The feedback evaluates actions in an environment.
hint: Ask how the learning system receives feedback.
trap: Not every game AI uses reinforcement learning; the described feedback mechanism determines the answer.
transfer: A game agent can improve action choices from observed rewards.

question: A company needs one model to interpret a product photo and answer a text question about it. Which capability is required?
options: A. Text-only generation | B. Multimodal understanding | C. Text embedding generation only | D. Speech transcription only
why: The model must understand both visual content and text to answer the request.
all_option_reasons: A. A text-only model cannot directly interpret the product image. | B. The model must understand both visual content and text to answer the request. | C. Text embeddings alone do not provide the requested image interpretation and response. | D. Speech transcription handles audio, not the product photo.
clues: photo and answer a text question: Two input/output modalities are involved.
hint: List the content formats that the model must handle.
trap: A model that generates images is not necessarily a model that understands image inputs.
transfer: Answering a question about a chart image requires processing both image and text.

question: An on-demand model charges per input and output token. Which change most directly reduces generation cost when answer quality remains acceptable?
options: A. Increase the maximum output for every request | B. Send all conversation history whether relevant or not | C. Remove unnecessary prompt text and cap output while checking quality | D. Fine-tune a larger model solely to increase its parameter count
why: For the stated token-priced model, reducing unnecessary input and output can lower cost while preserving the required quality.
all_option_reasons: A. A larger output allowance can increase token usage instead of reducing it. | B. Irrelevant history increases billed input without necessarily helping answer quality. | C. For the stated token-priced model, reducing unnecessary input and output can lower cost while preserving the required quality. | D. Increasing model size is not a direct remedy for excessive token use and may add costs.
clues: per input and output token: Both sides of the interaction can affect billing.
hint: Match the cost driver to the resource you can reduce.
trap: The shortest answer is not automatically best if it loses necessary information.
transfer: Trim irrelevant conversation history and test that answer quality remains sufficient.

question: A team begins with a broadly pretrained model that can be adapted for summarization, question answering and classification. What kind of starting model is this?
options: A. A foundation model | B. A classifier trained only for one fixed label set | C. A vector database index | D. A deterministic access policy
why: A foundation model is broadly pretrained and usable across multiple downstream tasks.
all_option_reasons: A. Broad pretraining and adaptability across tasks characterize a foundation model. | B. A narrow classifier does not match the described multi-task starting point. | C. An index stores representations; it is not the generative or predictive model. | D. An access policy enforces permissions rather than learning broad task capability.
clues: adapted for summarization, question answering and classification: The same starting model supports distinct tasks.
hint: Ask whether the starting point is a broadly trained model or a task-specific component.
trap: Confusing a store or a narrow classifier with a multi-purpose pretrained model.
transfer: A single broadly trained model may support both document summaries and question answering through different prompts.

question: Order these stages in a simplified foundation-model lifecycle, including optional adaptation.
options: A. Evaluate the adapted model against task requirements | B. Pre-train the foundation model | C. Deploy the model and collect feedback | D. Select and curate suitable training data | E. Adapt the model if the target task needs it
why: Curate data → pre-train → adapt if needed → evaluate → deploy and collect feedback.
all_option_reasons: A. Evaluate the result of training/adaptation before deployment. | B. Pre-training requires selected and prepared data. | C. Deployment follows evaluation; feedback can inform later iterations. | D. Data selection and curation support the subsequent training stage. | E. Task adaptation follows a base model and is not always necessary.
clues: including optional adaptation: Place adaptation after a base model exists and before its final task evaluation.
hint: Trace the dependencies from source data to a deployed model.
trap: The ordered exercise is a simplified dependency chain; real projects can iterate and evaluate at multiple points.
transfer: Evaluate the adapted model before production use and monitor feedback after deployment.

question: An assistant can call an inventory tool, inspect the returned stock level and then decide whether to call a supplier tool to meet a user goal. What behavior distinguishes it from a fixed one-step response?
options: A. Retrieving a static passage once | B. Choosing subsequent actions from tool results toward a goal | C. Converting input text into token IDs | D. Storing a file in object storage
why: Agentic behavior includes selecting actions and using observations to pursue a goal.
all_option_reasons: A. Retrieval can supply context but does not describe the action decision loop. | B. The assistant selects and adapts tool actions based on intermediate results. | C. Tokenization is part of model input processing, not the goal-directed loop. | D. Object storage does not choose the next action.
clues: decide whether to call a supplier tool: A later action depends on an earlier observation.
hint: Identify the decision loop rather than a component the system might use.
trap: Calling any chatbot or single retrieval step an agent merely because it uses an LLM.
transfer: A travel agent checks flight availability, then chooses a hotel search based on the selected destination.

question: A startup can invoke a foundation model through a managed API or host the model on its own inference servers. It has little operations capacity and variable traffic. What is a likely reason to start with the managed API?
options: A. It guarantees lower cost at every traffic level | B. It reduces the servers and scaling infrastructure the startup operates directly | C. It transfers all responsibility for output quality and access permissions to the provider | D. It ensures identical latency and model availability in every Region
why: A managed API can reduce direct infrastructure operations; compare actual cost and latency for the workload.
all_option_reasons: A. Costs depend on traffic and pricing; managed inference is not always cheaper. | B. The provider operates much of the inference infrastructure, fitting limited operations capacity. | C. The application owner still evaluates output and configures appropriate access. | D. Region, capacity and model choice can affect availability and latency.
clues: little operations capacity and variable traffic: The team values avoiding server management and scaling work.
hint: Distinguish an operational advantage from guarantees about cost, quality or Region.
trap: Assuming managed eliminates customer responsibilities or guarantees the lowest bill.
transfer: A small support team may start with managed inference, then reassess hosting when sustained high-volume demand changes its economics.

question: An assistant has access to a policy index, a conversation history and tool descriptions. Before each model call, the application chooses the relevant portions that fit the task and context window. What practice is this?
options: A. Context engineering | B. Fine-tuning on the entire history | C. Model distillation from a teacher | D. Increasing temperature for varied answers
why: Choosing and structuring relevant runtime information for a model call is context engineering.
all_option_reasons: A. Context engineering selects and structures useful runtime information for the request. | B. Fine-tuning changes model weights; selecting passages at request time does not. | C. Distillation trains a student model and does not describe runtime context selection. | D. Temperature changes sampling, not which documents or tools are supplied.
clues: chooses the relevant portions: Selection happens for the current request rather than in a training job.
hint: Ask whether information is being supplied at request time or learned into weights.
trap: Confusing runtime context assembly with training or sampling settings.
transfer: A claims assistant may include the latest policy section and only the recent messages needed for one case.

question: A team has a model and tools and wants an open-source SDK to build the agent’s reasoning loop. Hosting will be chosen separately. Which option best fits?
options: A. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime | B. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases | C. Strands Agents | D. Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management
why: Strands is the agent development SDK; runtime hosting, retrieval and prompt storage solve different needs.
all_option_reasons: A. Runtime hosts agent code but is not the requested open-source development SDK. | B. Knowledge Bases retrieves information; it does not provide the agent loop SDK. | C. Strands Agents is an open-source SDK for constructing model-driven agents with tools. | D. Prompt Management stores and versions prompts, a different part of the application.
clues: open-source SDK: The question asks for a development framework, not a deployed service.
hint: Separate building the agent loop from hosting, retrieval and prompt versioning.
trap: Confusing a framework used to build an agent with managed infrastructure that operates it.
transfer: A team can build in Strands locally, then choose a compatible runtime for deployment.

question: An agent already works in its chosen framework. The team needs a managed, framework-agnostic environment to host and run that agent without rebuilding its reasoning loop. Which AWS capability is the closest fit?
options: A. Strands Agents SDK | B. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime | C. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases | D. Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management
why: AgentCore Runtime is the managed hosting layer for the existing agent code.
all_option_reasons: A. Strands is a development SDK, not the managed runtime requested. | B. AgentCore Runtime hosts and runs agents built with various frameworks. | C. Knowledge Bases supports retrieval over data sources, not general agent hosting. | D. Prompt Management stores prompts, not the running agent process.
clues: already works in its chosen framework: The team wants to operate existing code, not adopt a new framework.
hint: Find the component that hosts the agent while preserving its chosen framework.
trap: Choosing a tool used by the agent rather than the environment that runs the agent.
transfer: A customer-support agent built in a third-party framework can run in AgentCore Runtime while using a separate knowledge base.

question: A product team wants an AI development environment that turns a feature request into reviewable requirements, design and implementation tasks before coding. Which tool is the most direct fit?
options: A. Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management | B. Strands Agents | C. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime | D. Kiro
why: Kiro’s spec workflow addresses the requested development process.
all_option_reasons: A. Prompt Management versions model prompts; it does not create a software feature specification workflow. | B. Strands builds agents, not the requested software development environment. | C. AgentCore Runtime operates agents rather than turning a feature request into a development plan. | D. Kiro supports specification-driven software development with requirements, design and tasks.
clues: reviewable requirements, design and implementation tasks: These are software specification artifacts rather than agent runtime components.
hint: Match the requested development workflow, not merely any AI-related AWS tool.
trap: Assuming an agent hosting service is also an IDE or spec planning tool.
transfer: A team can use Kiro to plan a billing feature, then review the generated design and test its implementation.

question: Two models pass a quality threshold on a representative support workload. The smaller model is cheaper but slower for the longest requests; the larger one is faster but costs more. What should the team do before choosing?
options: A. Choose the largest model because size is a reliable proxy for suitability | B. Compare latency and cost distributions against the actual service targets, then choose the fit | C. Choose the cheaper model using average cost alone | D. Choose the faster model using one demonstration request
why: Both models pass quality; compare the remaining constraints on representative traffic and service targets.
all_option_reasons: A. Model size is not a substitute for the stated workload measurements. | B. The choice depends on tail latency, traffic mix, cost and the agreed service targets. | C. An average bill can hide long-request latency that violates the service target. | D. One demonstration does not represent the workload or cost distribution.
clues: slower for the longest requests: Tail behavior can matter even when average performance looks good.
hint: Use the actual workload and service target rather than a single headline metric.
trap: Selecting by model size, average cost or one demo while ignoring the workload distribution.
transfer: A multilingual chatbot may need separate checks for long translated queries before selecting the cheaper model.

question: A support assistant must use a changing product manual and follow a demonstrated response format. The team will keep the existing model weights and cannot fit the entire manual in one prompt. Which TWO approaches jointly meet the requirements?
options: A. Retrieve relevant manual passages for each request | B. Fine-tune on pairs of customer questions and approved replies | C. Include a few demonstrations of the required format in the prompt | D. Continue pre-training on the complete manual | E. Cache a successful response and reuse it for similar requests
why: Retrieval supplies relevant manual evidence at request time, while few-shot examples demonstrate the format. Neither approach changes the model’s weights.
all_option_reasons: A. Retrieval selects relevant passages from the manual within the available context; its index must be kept current. | B. Fine-tuning can adapt responses but updates model weights, violating the stated constraint. | C. Few-shot demonstrations guide the requested format at inference time without training. | D. Continued pre-training changes model weights and does not meet the no-training constraint. | E. Reused responses can contain stale or mismatched facts and do not jointly provide current evidence and format demonstrations.
clues: existing model weights: Eliminate training-based changes. | changing product manual: The facts must come from updated request-time context.
hint: One approach must supply relevant facts; the other must demonstrate the format without training.
trap: Choosing two methods that address style but do not provide fresh product facts.
transfer: A lease assistant can retrieve the relevant contract section and use a few examples to produce a consistent summary format.

question: A model must label sentiment from an instruction with no demonstrations in the prompt. Which prompting technique is this?
options: A. Few-shot | B. Zero-shot | C. Distillation | D. Continuous pre-training
why: Zero-shot asks the model to perform the task without demonstrations.
all_option_reasons: A. Few-shot includes a small set of demonstrations. | B. Zero-shot asks the model to perform the task without demonstrations. | C. Distillation trains a student from a teacher. | D. Continuous pre-training changes model parameters with additional training.
clues: no demonstrations: Count examples rather than instructions.
hint: An instruction is not the same thing as a worked example.
trap: Zero-shot does not mean the prompt contains no guidance.
transfer: Ask for sentiment from an instruction alone, without demonstrations.

question: A document search system should retrieve passages about “ending a lease” when a user asks about “early termination.” Which comparison best supports this semantic match?
options: A. Compare exact file names only | B. Compare document creation dates only | C. Compare compatible query and passage embedding vectors | D. Compare S3 encryption key names
why: Vector similarity can retrieve related passages despite different surface wording.
all_option_reasons: A. File names may use different words from the user’s intent. | B. Dates measure recency, not semantic relatedness. | C. Embeddings can place related meanings near one another for vector search. | D. Encryption keys protect data rather than encode document meaning.
clues: “ending a lease”: The query and relevant passage may not share exact words.
hint: Choose the representation that can compare meaning across wording differences.
trap: Assuming exact text matching or metadata alone captures semantic similarity.
transfer: “Cancel my contract” may retrieve a section titled “termination rights” through embedding search.

question: A 200-page policy manual is indexed for RAG. The assistant needs to answer from the paragraph relevant to each question while keeping the context compact. Why split the manual into passages?
options: A. To remove the need to track the source document | B. To guarantee every answer is factually correct | C. To retrieve focused text that fits the model context with source metadata | D. To train the model weights each time the policy changes
why: Chunking supports retrieval of relevant passages within context limits; source links and validation remain necessary.
all_option_reasons: A. Chunks should retain useful source metadata for traceability. | B. Chunking can help retrieval but cannot guarantee grounding or correctness. | C. Focused chunks improve retrieval and use limited context more efficiently. | D. Indexing passages is retrieval, not weight training.
clues: 200-page policy manual: The whole document is too broad for each answer.
hint: Think about retrieval granularity and the size of runtime context.
trap: Treating chunking as a guarantee of truth or as retraining.
transfer: A lengthy product catalogue can be indexed by sections so a specific warranty passage is retrieved.

question: A RAG chatbot cites a policy paragraph that was replaced last month. What should the team investigate first?
options: A. Increase sampling temperature | B. Check source freshness and index synchronization | C. Increase the maximum response length | D. Switch to a larger model without checking the retrieved context
why: Check source versions, ingestion and index updates to determine why obsolete information was retrieved.
all_option_reasons: A. Temperature changes sampling behavior and does not refresh outdated documents. | B. Check source versions, ingestion and index updates to determine why obsolete information was retrieved. | C. Longer output can still repeat the same obsolete passage. | D. A larger model can receive and rely on the same stale context; inspect retrieval first.
clues: was replaced last month: The content used for grounding is outdated.
hint: Trace the answer back to the source and its ingestion process.
trap: A citation proves a source was referenced, not that the source is current.
transfer: Refresh the index when a policy document is superseded, then check the cited passage.

question: A prompt asks for a JSON object with three named fields. What most directly improves the chance of the desired format?
options: A. Describe only the topic and omit the field names | B. Specify the required schema and a valid example, then validate output | C. Use a higher temperature to encourage format variation | D. Repeat an ambiguous request several times without testing
why: Clear structure and a valid example improve guidance; programmatic validation still checks whether the response meets the contract.
all_option_reasons: A. Omitting field names leaves the required output structure ambiguous. | B. Clear structure and a valid example improve guidance; programmatic validation still checks whether the response meets the contract. | C. More variation does not directly improve adherence to an exact JSON structure. | D. Repeating ambiguity does not resolve it or verify valid JSON.
clues: three named fields: The desired structure should be explicit.
hint: Choose the change that removes ambiguity from the requested output.
trap: A well-written format instruction still needs output validation in production.
transfer: A schema example guides a JSON reply, while validation checks the actual output.

question: A model response must stop after a short answer. Which inference setting most directly limits generated length?
options: A. Maximum output tokens | B. Temperature | C. Top P | D. Number of few-shot examples
why: Maximum output tokens directly caps generation length, although a cap can truncate content.
all_option_reasons: A. Maximum output tokens directly caps generation length, although a cap can truncate content. | B. Temperature influences sampling variation, not a hard length cap. | C. Top P controls the candidate token distribution, not the maximum output length. | D. Examples can guide behavior but do not enforce a hard output-length limit.
clues: limits generated length: The control should act on output tokens.
hint: Separate inference settings from training and infrastructure settings.
trap: Truncating an answer is not the same as teaching the model to be concise.
transfer: Set a maximum generated-token budget and check that answers are not cut off.

question: Match each foundation-model evaluation technique to what it assesses.
options: A. BERTScore | B. BLEU | C. LLM-as-a-judge | D. ROUGE
why: BLEU is associated with translation overlap; ROUGE with summary overlap; BERTScore with semantic comparison; an LLM judge with rubric-based model assessment.
all_option_reasons: A. BERTScore uses contextual embeddings to compare generated and reference text. | B. BLEU uses n-gram precision with a brevity penalty and is commonly associated with translation. | C. An LLM judge evaluates responses against supplied criteria but can have its own biases and errors. | D. ROUGE measures overlap with reference text and is commonly used for summaries.
clues: evaluation technique: Distinguish reference overlap, semantic similarity and model-based judgment.
hint: Identify how each metric compares or judges the generated response.
trap: A good overlap score does not prove truth; a model judge also needs validation.
transfer: Use human review for nuanced usefulness, and task-specific metrics where suitable.

question: A RAG assistant retrieves a relevant policy passage but answers with a claim the passage does not support. Which evaluation approach best locates this failure?
options: A. Evaluate retrieval relevance and the generated answer’s support from the retrieved passage separately | B. Measure only the number of documents in the source bucket | C. Measure only the language model’s output tokens per second | D. Compare the answer to a reference using ROUGE alone
why: A RAG evaluation should examine both the retrieved evidence and whether the generated answer is grounded in it.
all_option_reasons: A. Separate retrieval and generation checks reveal that retrieval succeeded while grounding failed. | B. Document count does not show whether the answer is supported. | C. Throughput does not evaluate the claim or cited evidence. | D. Lexical overlap alone can miss an unsupported claim and does not isolate retrieval from generation.
clues: retrieves a relevant policy passage: The retrieval step may be correct even if generation misuses it.
hint: Separate what was retrieved from what the assistant asserted.
trap: Treating good retrieval or a surface text-overlap score as proof of a supported final answer.
transfer: A product assistant can retrieve the right warranty page yet invent a longer coverage period; check both retrieval and answer support.

question: An LLM judge rates a new answer style higher than the old one, but human reviewers repeatedly find unsupported claims in the new answers. What is the strongest next evaluation step?
options: A. Calibrate the judge and rubric against representative human-reviewed examples, including unsupported claims | B. Treat the judge score as ground truth because it is numerical | C. Remove the human-reviewed examples from the evaluation set | D. Increase the candidate model’s output length until the judge score improves
why: A judge model is another fallible evaluator; calibrate it against suitable human evidence and a clear rubric.
all_option_reasons: A. Calibration tests whether the judge’s scoring tracks the quality criterion that matters. | B. A numeric judge score can still reflect model error or rubric bias. | C. Removing contradictory evidence would hide the problem, not resolve it. | D. Longer answers can add more unsupported claims and do not validate the judge.
clues: human reviewers repeatedly find unsupported claims: The automated score conflicts with a relevant quality signal.
hint: Ask how to check whether the evaluator rewards the right behavior.
trap: Treating the judge’s score as objective truth because the scoring process is automated.
transfer: A summarization judge should be checked against human-reviewed cases with subtle omissions and fabricated details.

question: A refund agent retrieves the right policy but sometimes invokes the wrong tool and leaves the case unfinished. Which evaluation gives the clearest evidence about the application’s failure?
options: A. Measure only passage relevance in the retriever | B. Measure only the model’s answer similarity to a reference sentence | C. Replay representative end-to-end cases and check authorized tool calls and final task outcomes | D. Count the number of policy documents indexed
why: The failure is in tool execution and task completion, so evaluate the whole agent workflow.
all_option_reasons: A. Passage relevance cannot detect a wrong tool call after retrieval. | B. Text similarity may look good even when the refund workflow fails. | C. End-to-end traces reveal execution correctness and whether the task completes. | D. Document count says little about action safety or completion.
clues: invokes the wrong tool: The agent’s action path matters beyond the retrieved document.
hint: Trace the request through retrieval, selected action and observed outcome.
trap: Calling retrieval success equivalent to agent success.
transfer: A travel agent that finds the right fare still needs a correct, authorized booking outcome.

question: A team tests a prompt change for an assistant, but it cannot reproduce last week’s response or tell whether a regression came from the prompt or model setting. What should it record?
options: A. Only the latest prompt text | B. Versioned prompt and model settings linked to comparable evaluation results | C. Only the total number of generated tokens | D. Only the user rating of the newest response
why: Record prompt versions, relevant settings and evaluations so changes can be compared and reproduced.
all_option_reasons: A. The latest text alone loses the earlier version and configuration. | B. Versioned artifacts and comparable results support tracing a regression. | C. Token totals do not identify which prompt or model configuration changed. | D. One rating does not reconstruct the prior setup or isolate a regression.
clues: prompt or model setting: More than one change could explain the regression.
hint: Choose a record that preserves both the artifact and evidence for each run.
trap: Saving only the latest wording while treating evaluations as detached from their configuration.
transfer: A support assistant can compare two prompt variants against the same cases before a rollout.

question: A chatbot must answer using private company documents and show the supporting source passages. Which Bedrock capability best fits?
options: A. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases | B. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails alone | C. AWS Artifact | D. Amazon Comprehend
why: Knowledge Bases supports retrieving connected source material for grounded responses and source references.
all_option_reasons: A. Knowledge Bases supports retrieving connected source material for grounded responses and source references. | B. Guardrails provides safeguards but does not itself replace document ingestion and retrieval. | C. Artifact provides AWS compliance documents, not a general question-answering store for the company’s private policies. | D. Comprehend analyzes text; it is not the Bedrock retrieval-and-grounded-generation capability.
clues: supporting source passages: The answer must be grounded in the company’s own documents.
hint: Identify the retrieval-and-grounding requirement before selecting a service.
trap: Do not confuse AWS compliance reports with a knowledge base over your own business documents.
transfer: Retrieve private product manuals and return source references with an answer.

question: A team wants one place to document a model’s intended use, limitations and evaluation results. What fits?
options: A. A CloudTrail event log alone | B. A SageMaker Model Card | C. An IAM permission policy | D. An embedding vector index
why: A Model Card records key model details, intended use, limitations and evaluation information.
all_option_reasons: A. An activity log does not replace structured documentation of intended use and limitations. | B. A Model Card records key model details, intended use, limitations and evaluation information. | C. IAM policies define permissions rather than documenting the model’s intended use. | D. A vector index supports retrieval rather than serving as a model governance record.
clues: intended use, limitations: The goal is transparent model documentation.
hint: Choose the artifact that explains the model to stakeholders.
trap: A model card is evidence of documentation, not a certification of correctness.
transfer: Record intended use, limitations and evaluation results for a deployed model.

question: A model will serve three regions. One region has very few examples in both training and evaluation data. Before claiming comparable regional performance, which TWO actions most directly address this evidence gap?
options: A. Evaluate each region with an adequately sized, suitable held-out sample | B. Increase the size of the existing majority-region evaluation sample | C. Curate appropriately sourced examples for the underrepresented region and reassess after model changes | D. Apply the same confidence threshold across regions without collecting additional evidence | E. Report a population-weighted average of the existing regional scores
why: Suitable held-out evaluation measures regional outcomes, and representative data addresses the coverage gap. Reassess all regions after changes.
all_option_reasons: A. Adequate, suitable regional samples support meaningful comparisons without using training outcomes as proof. | B. More examples from the already well-represented region do not fill the missing region’s evidence gap. | C. Relevant representative data can address the coverage gap; separate evaluation must test the resulting model. | D. A shared threshold does not supply missing data or establish comparable performance. | E. A weighted average can hide poor performance in a small region and leaves the evidence gap unresolved.
clues: both training and evaluation data: The gap affects learning and the evidence used to assess it.
hint: Choose a measurement step and a representation step that address the missing region.
trap: Treating a large total dataset or a strong weighted average as proof of regional performance.
transfer: Adding more English examples does not establish reliable performance for a language missing from the test set.

question: A company runs millions of short, routine classification requests. A smaller model meets the measured quality and latency targets; a larger model uses more resources for the same workload. Which next step supports sustainability?
options: A. Keep the larger model solely because its parameter count is higher | B. Pilot the smaller suitable model and measure energy or resource use as well as quality | C. Double the output length to make the larger model’s answers more detailed | D. Run both models for every request indefinitely without a business need
why: A fit-for-purpose model and measured resource use can reduce unnecessary computation.
all_option_reasons: A. Parameter count alone does not justify extra computation. | B. Measure actual workload resource use while preserving the required quality and latency. | C. Longer output can increase resource use and does not address this classification need. | D. Unnecessary duplicate inference adds work without a justified outcome.
clues: smaller model meets the measured quality and latency targets: The smaller option is a plausible fit; verify its resource effect.
hint: Consider the whole workload rather than assuming a model size alone proves sustainability.
trap: Claiming environmental benefit from a smaller parameter count without measuring the actual workload.
transfer: A routine ticket classifier can be right-sized while more complex cases are routed for additional review.

question: An AI-assisted benefits decision is disputed by an applicant. Staff can inspect the model output, but the applicant receives only “denied” and has no correction route. What change best supports accountability?
options: A. Publish the full model weights and remove human review | B. Provide understandable case-specific reasons and a way to request human review or correction | C. Show a confidence score while keeping the decision final | D. Ask the applicant to submit the same request repeatedly until the output changes
why: A person affected by a consequential decision needs understandable reasons and an effective review path.
all_option_reasons: A. Weights alone do not explain an individual decision or give a remedy. | B. Meaningful reasons and a review path let a person challenge a possible mistake. | C. Confidence is not a decision justification or appeal mechanism. | D. Repeated submissions are not an accountable correction process.
clues: no correction route: The issue is not only explanation; the person needs a way to contest error.
hint: Consider what the affected person can understand and do after receiving the decision.
trap: Mistaking a technical transparency artifact or confidence score for meaningful recourse.
transfer: An insurance claimant should be told the relevant grounds and how to request a human reconsideration.

question: Which AWS service helps assess resource configurations against defined rules over time?
options: A. AWS Config | B. AWS CloudTrail | C. Amazon CloudWatch metrics | D. AWS Artifact
why: Config records resource configurations and evaluates them against rules.
all_option_reasons: A. Config records resource configurations and evaluates them against rules. | B. CloudTrail records supported API activity; that differs from evaluating configuration state against a rule. | C. Metrics monitor operational quantities rather than replacing resource configuration compliance checks. | D. Artifact supplies compliance documents rather than tracking your resource configurations over time.
clues: resource configurations against defined rules: The requirement is configuration compliance rather than API event history.
hint: Distinguish resource state from records of who called an API.
trap: Audit and compliance tools overlap in purpose but capture different evidence.
transfer: Check whether a resource configuration still meets a defined rule after a change.

question: A compliance reviewer needs AWS-provided SOC and ISO reports for a vendor assessment. The team also has its own application logs, but those are not the requested reports. Where should it obtain the AWS documents?
options: A. AWS CloudTrail | B. AWS Config | C. AWS Artifact | D. Amazon Macie
why: AWS Artifact supplies AWS compliance documents; customer logs and configuration evidence answer different questions.
all_option_reasons: A. CloudTrail records supported account activity; it is not the report portal. | B. Config evaluates customer resource configuration against rules. | C. Artifact provides access to AWS compliance reports and agreements. | D. Macie finds sensitive data in S3, not AWS auditor reports.
clues: AWS-provided SOC and ISO reports: The requested artifacts are AWS’s compliance documents.
hint: Separate provider compliance reports from evidence about your own resource behavior.
trap: Assuming a provider report proves the customer application itself is compliant.
transfer: A procurement review may request AWS SOC reports while also checking the customer’s own access logs.

question: A team uses a managed AWS AI service to process customer records. AWS operates the underlying infrastructure. Who must still decide and enforce which employees may send those records to the service?
options: A. AWS alone, because the infrastructure is managed | B. The customer, through its data-handling rules and appropriately scoped access controls | C. The foundation model, based on its confidence in each employee | D. The external browser used to view the application
why: Managed service use retains customer responsibility for data and access choices; exact duties depend on the service.
all_option_reasons: A. Managed infrastructure does not transfer every customer data and identity decision to AWS. | B. The customer retains decisions about permitted data use and who can access its resources. | C. Model confidence is not an authorization control. | D. A browser does not define the organization’s AWS permissions.
clues: which employees may send those records: This is an authorization and customer-data governance decision.
hint: Separate infrastructure operation from the customer’s identities, permissions and data policy.
trap: Assuming managed means all data and access decisions are handled by AWS.
transfer: A company using managed document analysis still decides who may upload payroll files.

question: An order assistant may read order status but must not issue refunds. Even if an injected instruction makes the model request a refund, which TWO controls independently restrict what can execute?
options: A. Use a runtime identity whose downstream permissions allow only order lookup | B. Put the no-refund rule in the system prompt and inspect its wording during testing | C. Authorize each tool call at the execution boundary against an approved read-only action set | D. Record refund attempts in an audit log and review them after execution | E. Require a high model-confidence score before executing a refund request
why: Least-privilege downstream permissions and execution-time authorization enforce the action boundary even when the model generates an unsafe request.
all_option_reasons: A. The actual credential must lack refund capability; hiding a tool while retaining broad credentials is insufficient. | B. Prompt instructions guide behavior but cannot serve as the permission boundary if the model requests a forbidden action. | C. The execution layer rejects operations outside the approved read-only set before any side effect occurs. | D. Logging helps detection and investigation but does not prevent the prohibited refund. | E. A confident unsafe request is still unsafe; a confidence threshold does not authorize an action.
clues: restrict what can execute: The controls must block the action outside the model’s text decision.
hint: Distinguish prevention before a side effect from model guidance and after-the-fact detection.
trap: Confusing an instruction, an audit record or model confidence with an enforceable permission.
transfer: A reporting assistant needs read-only access to accounting data even if its prompt says never to edit records.

question: A team has labeled customer-churn rows in a table and a folder of untagged product photos. Which description of these inputs is accurate?
options: A. Both sets are labeled, structured data because they are stored digitally | B. The rows are labeled, structured data; the photos are unstructured and currently unlabeled | C. The photos are structured data because each file has a name | D. Neither set can be used in AI until converted to text
why: The table has a schema and target labels. The photos are image content without target labels in the scenario.
all_option_reasons: A. Digital storage does not make content tabular or supply a target label. | B. The rows have fields and churn targets; the images lack supplied class labels. | C. File metadata does not make the image pixels a structured table for this task. | D. Image models can use photos; converting them to text is not inherently required.
clues: labeled customer-churn rows: The rows have known target answers; the photos do not.
hint: Separate data shape from whether the desired target is supplied.
trap: Assuming a filename labels the image for the intended prediction.
transfer: A spreadsheet of tagged support tickets is structured and labeled; a folder of untagged voice notes is unstructured and unlabeled.
